runs.t: Red Hat Enterprise Linux System Administration I | Study file

This chapter teaches you to log in to other Linux machines safely with SSH. You learn to run commands remotely, to log in with keys instead of passwords, and to make the SSH server safer by blocking root logins and password logins.

Known hosts files keep one server key per line, and you must update them if a server's key changes.
Think of an address book. If someone moves or changes their ID, you must fix the old entry or you cannot reach them cleanly.

If a server's public key changes, for example after a hard drive failure or a planned replacement, edit the known hosts files so the old entry is replaced with the new key. Otherwise you get errors when you log in.
Each key is on one line. The first field lists host names and IP addresses that share the key. The second field is the encryption algorithm. The last field is the key itself.

Key-based login proves who you are with a pair of keys, so you do not type a password each time.
Think of a lock and a key. The server holds the lock (your public key). You hold the key (your private key). The lock can be copied and shown to anyone, but only your key opens it.

Think of a master key. It is safer if the master key cannot be used from outside.
It is good practice to block direct root login from remote systems. The name

exists on every Linux system, so an attacker only needs to guess a password. Root has no limits, so a break-in does the most damage. And it is hard to audit who logged in as root. If users log in as a normal user and then switch to root, that creates a log event.
